name: Password Hashing
intent: Store passwords so that a stolen database does not give attackers the passwords: use a unique salt per user and a deliberately slow hash.
scenario: A shop stores customer passwords. One night its user table is copied by an attacker. What they can do with that copy depends entirely on how the passwords were stored.
problem: Databases leak. If passwords are stored in plain text, every account is lost immediately, along with every other site where people reused the password. Hashing helps, but fast hashes such as SHA-256 let an attacker try billions of guesses per second, and identical passwords produce identical hashes that can be cracked once for everyone.

howItWorks.title: Never store the password, store a hash
howItWorks.text: A hash function turns the password into a fixed-size fingerprint that cannot be reversed. At login you hash what the user typed and compare it to the stored value. Nobody, including your own staff, can read the original.

howItWorks.title: Add a unique random salt for every user
howItWorks.text: A salt is random data stored next to the hash and mixed into it. Two users with the same password then get different hashes, which defeats precomputed tables of hashes (rainbow tables) and forces the attacker to attack each account separately.

howItWorks.title: Use a hash that is slow on purpose
howItWorks.text: General-purpose hashes are built for speed, which is exactly what an attacker wants. Password hashes such as Argon2, scrypt, bcrypt and PBKDF2 are tunable: a work factor makes each guess cost real time (and, for Argon2 and scrypt, memory). A login that takes 100 ms is invisible to a user but makes mass guessing impractical.

howItWorks.title: Tune and upgrade the work factor over time
howItWorks.text: Hardware gets faster, so raise the cost periodically. Store the algorithm and cost beside each hash, and when a user logs in successfully with an old setting, re-hash their password with the new one.

howItWorks.title: Defend the login, too
howItWorks.text: Slow hashing protects stolen data, not online guessing. Add rate limiting and lockouts to the login, support multi-factor authentication, reject known breached passwords, and compare hashes in constant time.

pros: A leaked database does not reveal passwords directly
Salting stops one precomputed table from cracking everyone
Slow hashing makes each guess expensive for the attacker
Cost can be raised as computers get faster
cons: Each login costs real CPU (and memory) time on your servers
Weak passwords such as '123456' still fall quickly whatever the hash
Needs migration planning to raise the cost or change algorithm
Easy to implement wrongly: homemade schemes are weaker than standard ones
whenToUse: Any system where users log in with a password you verify yourself
Choose Argon2id where available, otherwise scrypt, bcrypt or PBKDF2 with a high iteration count
whenNotToUse: Hashing API keys or tokens that are long random values: a fast hash is fine there, since guessing is impossible
Instead of delegating login to a trusted identity provider, if that is an option
pitfalls: Using MD5, SHA-1 or plain SHA-256 for passwords
One site-wide salt (or none), instead of a random salt per user
Writing your own scheme, such as hashing twice or mixing in a secret by hand
Truncating or silently limiting password length, or logging passwords

roles.label: User
roles.description: Chooses a password and types it at login.

roles.label: Application
roles.description: Salts and hashes the password, and compares at login.

roles.label: Database
roles.description: Stores the salt and hash, never the password.
